title: A letter for after
hookLine: a letter to be read after you're gone
last: A KNOT TIED IN A HANDKERCHIEF.

lines: TO BE OPENED AFTER I'M GONE.
cards: An envelope in a drawer, with one line on the front: to be opened after I'm gone. Inside there's no list of bank accounts, nothing about who gets the good chairs.

Just a page about what the writer learned, what they hope for, what they'd like forgiven. In Jewish tradition this kind of letter has a name, an ethical will, and some families still write and keep them.
The idea is far older than envelopes, and a few people in old books said one out loud.

teach.b: First, Jacob gathers his sons. In Genesis, the old man calls his family to his bed: "Gather yourselves together, that I may tell you that which shall befall you in the last days."
What follows is a long speech to each son by name. Some of it is blessing and some of it is blunt. It isn't a will about property.
It's a father saying who he thinks each of them is.

Second, a farewell. In the second letter to Timothy, the writer sounds like someone near the end: "the time of my departure is at hand. I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith."
Some readers hear the whole letter as a farewell, written for after.
Third, a will made of words. The Hebrew word for a will is tsavaah, and the ethical will borrows it for something different: not who gets what, but what mattered. Some are a few sentences long.
Some are pages of advice, apology and thanks. Rabbis wrote them, and so did ordinary parents.
Nobody needs to write the whole letter today. A first line is enough to find out what you'd want to say. And once a line is written for after, it has a way of asking whether it could be said now.

how: In Jewish tradition, an ethical will, a tsavaah, is a letter of values, blessings and requests left for family; some people of other paths also write letters to be read after their death, sometimes kept with a legal will.

practice: Think of one person who might one day read a letter from you, and without planning the whole thing, let the first lines come: what you hope for them, one thing you learned, one thing you're grateful for.
Write two or three sentences on paper or your phone, no more, or if nothing comes, write their name and sit with it. Then put it somewhere safe, or simply let it go.
